newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's National Assembly ends military service.
newsitem.headline: France's National Assembly ends military service.

text.p: France's National Assembly voted on Wednesday to end compulsory military service.
The government bill will create an all-professional armed forces by 2002 but allows conscription, introduced by the Revolutionaries of 1789, to be restored if needed for national defence.

The unpopular present law requires fit men to serve 10 months' military duty. As a concession to conservatives, it will be replaced by a five-day "citizens' meeting" for all young men and, after the first few years, for young women as well.
That will enable the state to assess the young people's fitness for service, in case a call-up is ever needed, and give them a course of lectures on patriotism and their duties to the Republic.
The bill also provides for volunteers to serve for nine to 24 months either in the armed forces, or as social workers in France or humanitarian workers and technicians abroad.
It was approved by a show of hands on a second reading and will go to the Senate (upper house) next month. Both houses have big centre-right majorities
Socialists and Communists opposed the bill and said they would ask the Constitutional Council to check whether it may breach the 1958 constitution.
The reform is part of President Jacques Chirac's plan for an all-professional armed forces that would be easier to send outside France's borders.
Professionals already make up most of the air force and navy and a sizeable part of the army.
